set.t: Sarcophagus with Christ, Peter and the Apostles
set.original_title: Sarcophage au Christ, Pierre et Apôtres (Ra 507)

summary: Along the front of this marble chest, framed by columns, Christ stands at the centre among ten apostles who turn toward him in pairs, many holding scrolls. The gabled lid, carved with overlapping scales like roof tiles, bears at its centre the chi-rho, the monogram formed from the first Greek letters of Christ's name. The whole presents Christ as teacher and Lord surrounded by the college of apostles, an image of the Church gathered around him in hope of eternal life.
facts: According to the museum, the lid did not originally belong to this chest, though it probably also came from Saint-Sernin; an inscription on its back records its reuse in 1754 for the tomb of a Toulouse merchant, Antoine Vigniaux.
In the 1770s the chest decorated the garden of Count Jean Dubarry's town house opposite Saint-Sernin, where it was nicknamed the 'Tomb of Jean-Jacques Rousseau'.

The hole drilled through the middle of the front, visible below Christ, is thought by the museum to have caused the crack that runs through the same spot; the short sides show a shepherd with his sheep and a lion hunt.
notes: POP dates the work to the 4th–5th century (worklist: 4th century). Wikidata's English description calls it 'bronze'; it is marble. The place of manufacture is not stated by the museum; only the findspot (the old 'cemetery of the nobles' at Saint-Sernin) is recorded.

set.t: Early Christian Sarcophagus Front with Christ, Peter, Paul and Apostles

summary: Seven arched niches, separated by slender columns with simple Corinthian capitals, run along this sarcophagus front. In the central niche stands a youthful, beardless Christ wearing the toga, his right hand at his breast and a scroll in his left; Peter and Paul turn toward him from the neighbouring niches, and pairs of apostles converse on either side, one of them taking a scroll from a book-box at his feet. The museum reads the central group as a variant of the Roman 'Traditio Legis', Christ giving the new Law to his apostles.
facts: The museum notes that the corner reinforcements left inside the chest when it was hollowed out are characteristic of the sarcophagi of southwestern France.
Its left short side shows Abraham about to sacrifice Isaac, a scene read by early Christians as a type of Christ's sacrifice and of salvation.
According to the museum's record it was reused in the Middle Ages to frame a church portal, so the place of its first use is unknown.
notes: POP: '4e quart 4e siècle ; 5e siècle'. The record names Saint-Michel-du-Touch (Toulouse) as findspot; the precise church where it was reused is only partly legible in the record as fetched. Identification of Peter and Paul follows the museum.

set.t: The Reider Panel: The Women at the Tomb and the Ascension of Christ

summary: In this finely carved ivory panel, three veiled women approach from the lower right, greeted by the angel seated before the tomb, a two-storey building crowned by a domed rotunda, while two guards slump against it. Above, the risen Christ, haloed and holding a scroll, strides up a hill and grasps the hand of God reaching from the clouds, as two disciples below cower or look up in awe. It is one of the oldest known figurative images of the Resurrection and Ascension.
facts: The panel was acquired for the Bavarian National Museum in 1860 from the Bamberg collector Martin von Reider, after whom it is named; it is the oldest work on display in the museum (inv. MA 157).
Drill holes at the four corners suggest it was once set into the cover of a liturgical book.
The tomb building has been discussed as a possible reflection of the shrine over Christ's tomb in the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem, consecrated in 335.
notes: Date c. 400 and origin Rome or Milan per German Wikipedia and the Commons file description; worklist had '4th century'.

summary: Twisted columns divide the front of this sarcophagus into five scenes of the Passion, told as a triumph. At the left Simon of Cyrene carries the cross; next a soldier sets a wreath, not a crown of thorns, on the head of the young Christ; at the right Christ is led before Pilate, who sits in thought as a servant brings water to wash his hands. In the centre, the cross is crowned by the chi-rho in a victor's wreath, with doves on its arms and two stunned soldiers below: the Resurrection shown not as a scene but as a sign of victory.
facts: The Vatican Museums record that it comes from the cemetery of Domitilla on the Via Ardeatina and date it to about 350 (inv. 31525).
The museum interprets the crowning with thorns as transformed into a crowning with a jewelled diadem, so that the Passion is shown as glorious.
No crucified Christ appears: in the mid-4th century the cross with the chi-rho stood for the Resurrection (Anastasis), while the stunned soldiers allude to the guards at the tomb.
notes: Commonly known as the 'Passion sarcophagus' (formerly Lateran 171).

set.l: Catacomb of Via Latina (Via Dino Compagni), Rome

summary: Within an arched niche, Christ in a white pallium stands at the head of a great crowd, stretching out his hand with a slender rod toward a small temple-like tomb at the top of a flight of steps. The packed ranks of witnesses, continuing onto the adjoining wall, give this Raising of Lazarus an unusual sense of public drama. In a burial chamber, the scene proclaimed Christ's power over death and the hope of resurrection for those laid to rest there.
facts: The Via Latina catacomb (Via Dino Compagni) was a private underground cemetery, discovered by chance during building work in the mid-1950s; it was in use for only about fifty years, from the early 4th century to around 350–360.
Its paintings mix Christian and pagan subjects, suggesting that not all the families buried there had become Christian, which has led scholars to call it a 'picture gallery of the 4th century'.
The Web Gallery of Art notes that the small temple-like building (aedicula) stands as a metaphor for the grave of Lazarus, opposite the figure of Christ commanding him to rise.

links.label: Wikipedia (Italian): Ipogeo di via Dino Compagni

notes: The specific cubiculum was not confirmed. A faint figure and a column painted higher up in the lunette were not identified and are not described.

reject_reason: Duplicate: this photograph shows the sarcophagus chest Ra 809 b (catalogued separately as Q104173756 in this batch) with the 'Queen Pédauque' lid Ra 501 displayed on top (already in the pilot batch as Q104173683).
notes: Wikidata Q25492374 combines both inventory numbers (Ra 809 b and Ra 501; POP 05630000090 and 05630030199). The cleaner museum photographs of each part are kept under Q104173756 and Q104173683.

set.t: Early Christian Sarcophagus Front with Christ Teaching among the Apostles

summary: Under a row of gabled and arched canopies carried on twisted columns, seven bearded and robed figures stand in niches. In the central niche Christ raises his right hand as he teaches, a box of scrolls (scrinium) at his feet, while the apostles around him hold scrolls and books or turn toward one another. The scrolls, borrowed from Roman imagery, signified knowledge of the true faith received from Christ the teacher.
facts: The chest was reused in the Middle Ages as a lintel over the door of the church of Saint-Michel-du-Touch, north of Toulouse; only the front and the beginnings of the short sides survive.
In 1777 local antiquaries took its figures for the decurions who formed the senate of Roman Toulouse.
The museum displays it with the 'Queen Pédauque' lid, which very probably belongs to it but was itself reused as a lintel at the church of La Daurade.
notes: The museum mentions a scrinium at Christ's feet and at those of the apostle in the last arcade on the left; the thumbnail shows boxes in the first and fourth niches. Christ is identified by position and gesture per the museum's description; he is not haloed.

set.m: Ivory on a walnut framework; later silver lock plate

summary: Every face of this ivory box is crowded with small reliefs. On the front, as seen here, a young beardless Christ teaches at the centre, seated among his listeners; at the left he turns to the kneeling woman who touched his garment, and at the right he appears with sheep at a doorway, usually read as the parable of the lost sheep. Above runs a row of medallion busts of the apostles, and around the main scenes are Old Testament episodes such as Jonah and Susanna, chosen to echo the Gospel stories.
facts: It is a virtually unique survival of a complete Early Christian ivory box, with 36 subjects drawn from both Testaments.
Shield emblems carved on the soldiers have been identified with a unit of the Palatine Guard stationed in Milan in the late 4th century, supporting a Milanese origin in the time of St Ambrose.
Dismantled and displayed flat in the 19th century, the casket was reassembled in 1928; its silver lock plate is a later addition, probably of the 8th century.
notes: Scene identifications on the front middle register follow Watson (1981) as summarised on Wikipedia; the central scene has also been read as Christ teaching the apostles or Christ among the doctors. Worklist date '350s' changed to 'late 4th century' (one theory places it soon after 386).

summary: In a row of shell-topped niches beneath a frieze of vines with harvesting putti, the apostles stand in pairs as Christ, at the centre, raises his right hand. This is the 'traditio legis', Christ giving the Law to St Peter as leader of the Church, with St Paul standing beside to acknowledge Peter's authority. Christ's face has been worn away, but his commanding gesture still holds the composition together.
facts: The Met explains that the Church of Rome developed this image in the late 4th century to stress the primacy of St Peter, traditionally the first bishop of Rome, and that it spread widely through western Europe.
Besides Peter and Paul, four further apostles survive on this fragment.
The scene is set within a traditional Roman sarcophagus form: niches framed by columns with putti in vine scrolls above.
notes: The scroll offered to Peter, mentioned by the Met, is not clearly legible in the thumbnail.

reject_reason: Not a figural depiction of Christ: the gold-glass roundel shows only Saints Peter and Paul (labelled PETRVS and PAVLVS) flanking a column topped by the chi-rho monogram; Christ is represented solely by his name-symbol.
notes: Met 16.174.3 (late 4th century). Could be reconsidered if the collection decides to include Christograms as 'symbolic depictions', but per the brief only clear depictions (e.g. the Lamb) qualify.

reject_reason: Duplicate: the same ceiling fresco (Christ enthroned between Peter and Paul, with the Lamb and four martyrs below) as the pilot entry wga:zearly/1/2mural/2marcell/marcel11, photographed after restoration.
notes: This WGA photograph (marcel12) is the clearer, post-restoration image showing the whole vault with the alpha and omega and martyrs' names legible; consider using it as the image for the pilot entry marcel11. WGA dates it 400–20.

summary: Woven in red and cream on this fragile band are the first events of Christ's life, set within little architectural frames and read from right to left: the Annunciation, the bathing of the newborn Christ, the Nativity with the Child lying in a stone manger, and the Adoration of the Shepherds. Though only fragments survive, the clear outlines of figures and buildings remain legible. A band like this may once have adorned a tunic, carrying the Gospel story on everyday dress.
facts: The Met notes that the bathing of the Christ Child was a popular motif not recorded in the Gospel texts.
It is woven in warp-faced compound twill of wool, linen and silk, and was made in Syria though found in Egypt.
The band came to the Met in 1890 as a gift of George F. Baker.

links.label: Wikipedia: Nativity of Jesus in art

notes: Scene identifications follow the Met; individual scenes are hard to make out in the small thumbnail.

summary: On the round disc of this red earthenware oil lamp, the haloed Christ stands holding a cross-staff, treading underfoot the lion, the dragon, the asp and the basilisk, while angels fly at either side; christograms in circles and chevrons decorate the rim. Small mould-made lamps like this were the everyday light of early Byzantine North Africa, and the image of Christ victorious over evil was thought to protect the lamp's owner.
facts: The Met notes that such lamps were made from double moulds and burned castor or sesame oil with a wick of plant fibre or linen.
The four beasts come from the Latin text of Psalm 91 (90):13, read in the early Church as Christ's triumph over Satan.
Christ treading on the beasts was a variant of the 'Christ in Triumph' image of the risen Christ, found in Late Antique and early medieval art but never common.

links.label: Wikipedia: Christ treading on the beasts

notes: The disc is worn and the figures are hard to read in the photograph; the description follows the Met.

summary: In a rocky green landscape beneath a starry blue vault, the young Christ sits among six sheep, reaching across to touch one that turns toward him. He wears a golden tunic with a purple mantle and a golden halo, and holds a tall golden cross instead of a shepherd's crook. The image fuses the gentle shepherd of the Gospel with the majesty of a ruler, one of the most beloved mosaics of the 5th century.
facts: The lunette is set over the north entrance of the building, built between 425 and 450 as a chapel adjoining the church of Santa Croce in Ravenna.
Despite its name, the empress Galla Placidia was not buried here; she died in Rome in 450, and the tradition of her burial in Ravenna dates from the 13th century.
The figure of a shepherd carrying a sheep was adopted from ancient art into Christian funerary art from the late 3rd century; here the shepherd is in imperial purple and gold.

set.t: Diptych Leaf or Book-Cover Plaque with Two Apostles and a Medallion of Christ
set.original_title: Diptyque ou plaque de reliure : deux apôtres entourant un médaillon du Christ
set.l: Musée du Louvre, Paris (Department of Decorative Arts)
set.m: Elephant ivory, low relief, traces of inlay (blue beads in the eyes)

summary: Two haloed apostles stand face to face, each holding a book and wrapped in a heavy mantle: at the left a young man with curly hair, of the type of St John, at the right a bearded, balding figure resembling St Peter, who points upward. Between their heads, a bearded Christ appears in a round medallion, the still centre of their conversation. The panel shows the apostles as witnesses whose testimony points to Christ.
facts: It forms a pair with a second Louvre plaque (OA 3850 bis) of identical design; the museum notes neither has hinge marks, so they may have been made to decorate a manuscript binding rather than as a true diptych.
Around 1100 the two plaques were joined and reused for a secular purpose: their backs were engraved with the board of a tric-trac (backgammon-type) game.
It was bought at the Ernest Odiot sale in Paris in 1889.
notes: Inventory discrepancy: Wikidata and the Commons filename give 'OA 3850' and link the Louvre record for OA 3223 (cl010113299); comparing the Louvre photographs, the image shown is OA 3223 (no inscriptions), not the inscribed companion OA 3850 bis, which came from the Musée Crozatier (Le Puy) by exchange in 1894. Wikidata's 'Musée Crozatier' location belongs to the companion. Place of making given by the Louvre as Italy or Gaul (?).

set.t: Plaque with the Denial of Peter, Peter's Remorse and Christ Led to Pilate
set.original_title: Plaque latérale d'un feuillet en cinq parties : Le Reniement de saint Pierre ; le Christ emmené chez Pilate
set.l: Musée du Louvre, Paris (Department of Decorative Arts)
set.m: Elephant ivory, low relief, drilled eyes

summary: This narrow ivory strip tells the night of Christ's betrayal in three scenes. At the top a servant-girl points accusingly at Peter in the courtyard of the high priest; in the middle Peter sits weeping, head in hand, with the cock perched before him; at the bottom the haloed Christ is led away between soldiers toward Pilate. The juxtaposition sets Peter's human weakness beside Christ's calm acceptance of his Passion.
facts: It is a side panel from a five-part ivory leaf, of the kind assembled around a larger central plaque.
The Louvre bought it in 1895 from the collector Charles Mannheim.
The cock recalls Christ's prophecy that Peter would deny him three times before the cock crowed.
notes: The Louvre identifies the lowest scene as Christ led to Pilate (Wikidata/Commons title: 'arrest of Christ'). Date and Ravenna attribution are given by the Louvre with a query, on stylistic grounds.

set.t: Amulet with Christ and the Woman with the Issue of Blood

summary: Incised into a polished oval of hematite and set in a silver mount, a tall haloed Christ stands at the right while a small figure below reaches toward him, beside lines of Greek inscription. The inscriptions identify the subject as the woman healed of a flow of blood when she touched Christ's garment. Worn close to the body, the amulet invoked that healing for its owner.
facts: The Met notes that hematite was believed to stop the flow of blood, and was a favourite stone for amulets concerned with women's reproductive health.
On the reverse a woman stands in the orant (prayer) pose.
It was a gift of J. Pierpont Morgan in 1917.
notes: The inscription is not transcribed here because it was not verified letter by letter. The kneeling woman is small and unclear in the photograph.

summary: On a gold ground above a flowering meadow, a bearded Christ in imperial purple sits on a jewelled throne with a red cushion, raising his right hand in blessing and holding a sceptre. Four angels in white, with haloes and long staffs, stand two by two on either side like a heavenly court. Christ appears here as King of Heaven, toward whom the procession of martyrs along the wall below advances.
facts: The group stands at the end of the south (right) wall, where a procession of 26 martyrs led by St Martin moves from Theodoric's palace toward the enthroned Christ; facing it on the north wall the Virgin and Child sit enthroned among four angels.
The church was built by the Ostrogothic king Theodoric as his palace church and dedicated in 504 to Christ the Redeemer.
The mosaics were restored in the mid-19th century by Felice Kibel.
notes: WGA dates it c. 500; the processions of martyrs on the same wall belong to the later, post-Arian redecoration of the 560s, the date of the enthroned Christ group itself was not independently confirmed. The mosaics were restored in the 19th century.

summary: Carved around this small round ivory box, a youthful Christ sits enthroned at the centre, flanked by the bearded Saints Peter and Paul, while other disciples bring forward loaves of bread with baskets at their feet. The miracle of the loaves was understood by the early Church as a sign of the bread of the Eucharist, and such boxes may have served in the Divine Liturgy.
facts: According to the Met, the box was made in North Africa, while its lid was made in Spain.
Traces of polychromy survive, and coloured inlays decorate the lid.
It came to the Met in 1917 as a gift of J. Pierpont Morgan.
notes: The Met cites Mark 8:1–6 (feeding of the four thousand); the scene could equally evoke the feeding of the five thousand.

reject_reason: Christ is not depicted: the pyxis shows women in prayer and women with censers approaching a domed shrine with an altar (the empty tomb); there is no figure of Christ.
notes: Met 464499. The Met relates the scene to Luke 24:1–10 (the women at the empty tomb).

summary: This tiny gold clasp holds at its centre a beaded medallion incised with the Virgin, her head veiled and haloed, and the Christ Child in a roundel before her breast, flanked by small crosses. Designed to be worn, it expressed its owner's devotion to Mary as Theotokos, the Mother of God, who bears Christ to the world.
facts: An inscription on the reverse, according to the Met, expresses the owner's devotion to the Virgin as Theotokos.
The Met notes that crosses appear on Byzantine jewellery by the 5th century, while images of the Virgin, saints and angels became popular in the 6th.
It was a gift of Helen Miller Gould in 1910.
notes: The Child is very small in the medallion; his presence is visible in the photograph. The inscription is not transcribed.

summary: Though heavily damaged, this limestone frieze still shows Christ enthroned under an arch at the centre, stretching out his right hand over a heap of baskets. Angels stand at his left and right, and beyond them apostles or saints hold books and raise their hands as if preaching. The baskets recall the twelve that were left over when Christ fed the five thousand.
facts: It is said to come from Bawit in Middle Egypt, site of a major early monastery.
The fragment is about a metre long and weighs some 51 kg.
It came to the Met in 1910 (Rogers Fund).

summary: Around the bowl of this silver incense burner, a medallion shows the bust of a youthful Christ with short curly hair and a halo, between figures of archangels. When incense rose from the censer during worship, the image placed the liturgy in the presence of Christ among his heavenly attendants.
facts: The Met notes that Christ is shown young to emphasise his divine vitality rather than his suffering, while the cross in his halo signals his identity.
A Greek inscription reads 'Of Saint John of the village of Attaroutha', naming the church to which it belonged.
It belongs to the Attarouthi Treasure, a group of liturgical silver from a village in Syria, acquired by the Met in 1986.
notes: Only one side is visible in the thumbnail; the archangels are partly seen.

summary: On this large silver chalice, a gilded arcade frames standing figures; here Christ, haloed and holding a book, raises his right hand in blessing beneath an arch, with a Greek inscription running around the rim above. The Met notes that the chalice carries images of Christ and the Virgin with saints and archangels, so that when it was raised at the Eucharist the congregation saw Christ's own image on the cup of his blood.
facts: Its Greek dedication asks prayers for the repose of the soul of Anastasia and the salvation of John, deacon of Saint Stephen of the village of Attarathion, according to the Met.
The cup holds about 1.5 litres, a generous size that, as the Met suggests, could be seen by a large congregation.
It is one of several chalices in the Attarouthi Treasure (Met 1986.3.5).
notes: Met object ID 466139, accession 1986.3.5 (identified via the Commons file).

summary: On the swelling body of this tall silver flask, partly gilded, the archangel Gabriel strides ahead leading the three Magi with their gifts toward the Christ Child, who sits on his mother's lap beneath the guiding star. Flasks of this kind may have been used as containers in a church, and the Magi were a favourite subject on early Byzantine objects linked to pilgrimage.
facts: The Met notes that only the Armenian Infancy Gospel describes the archangel as the Magi's guide.
It stands about 31.5 cm high.
Met accession 1984.196.
notes: The relief is too small in the thumbnail to confirm details; description follows the Met. 'c' set only to the Met's 'Byzantine' culture; no place of manufacture is given.

set.m: Ivory panels on a wooden frame

summary: This bishop's throne is entirely sheathed in carved ivory. On the front, John the Baptist, holding a medallion of the Lamb of God, stands between the four evangelists beneath Maximian's monogram, framed by vines inhabited by animals; on the high rounded back, panels tell the story of Christ's infancy and life, and on the sides the story of Joseph. Christ is thus present both as the Lamb proclaimed by the Baptist and in the Gospel scenes behind the bishop's head.
facts: It was made for Archbishop Maximian of Ravenna, who is named by his monogram on the front, and is the largest single surviving Late Antique work in ivory.
Of the 24 panels on the back, only 16 survive or have been restored.
Scholars still debate whether it was carved in Constantinople or Alexandria; differences in style suggest several carvers.
notes: The individual back panels are small in the thumbnail; Christ's appearances there were not individually confirmed from the image. Dating c. 545–553 per Wikipedia.

set.t: Christ Multiplying the Loaves and Fishes

summary: Against a gold ground, a young, beardless Christ in imperial purple stands with arms outstretched between four apostles; with one hand he blesses the loaves held out by the disciple at the left, and with the other the fishes held by the disciple at the right. Calm and frontal, Christ gives rather than performs, and the scene became an image of the Eucharistic bread that he still provides.
facts: It belongs to the cycle of 13 small panels of Christ's miracles and parables along the upper north wall, in which Christ is always young and beardless; on the facing wall, scenes of the Passion show him bearded.
These panels date from the time of Theodoric the Great, whose palace church was dedicated in 504.
The scenes are thought to follow the Gospel readings used in the church during Lent.
notes: WGA title 'Christ between Four Apostles' made more specific; the miracle is identified by WGA itself.

summary: At the centre of this five-part ivory leaf, an emperor on a rearing horse triumphs over a barbarian, while Earth bows at his foot and conquered peoples bring tribute below. In the upper panel, two flying angels hold up a medallion with the bust of a young, curly-haired Christ, raising his hand in blessing and holding a cross-sceptre. Christ reigns above while the emperor acts as his representative on earth.
facts: It is the only nearly complete surviving leaf of an imperial diptych; only the right-hand plaque is missing.
The emperor is usually identified as Justinian, though Anastasius has also been proposed; the prominence given to Christ blessing the emperor supports a Justinianic date.
The antiquary Peiresc gave it to Cardinal Francesco Barberini in 1625; the Louvre acquired it in 1899. Names of the kings of Austrasia are inscribed on the back.
notes: Louvre dates it 525–550; worklist year 525 adjusted to the middle of the range.

summary: A gilded openwork shell of fruited grapevine encloses a plain silver inner cup. Within the loops of the vine sit twelve figures holding scrolls, accompanied by birds, a lamb, a rabbit and an eagle; two of them, the most youthful, are thought to be images of Christ. Once hailed as the Holy Grail, the object is now seen as a fine 6th-century liturgical vessel, perhaps a standing lamp.
facts: When it surfaced in the early 20th century, its inner cup was claimed to be the cup of the Last Supper; it was exhibited as the Holy Grail at the 1933 Chicago World's Fair, a claim never substantiated.
The Met notes that its shape most closely resembles 6th-century standing lamps, perhaps alluding to Christ's words 'I am the light of the world'.
It has been argued to belong to a treasure of the church of Saint Sergios at Kaper Koraon, southeast of Antioch.
notes: Christ's presence rests on the Met's statement that two of the twelve figures 'are thought to be' Christ; they cannot be distinguished in the thumbnail. The other ten have been read as apostles or classical philosophers. Authenticity has at times been questioned.

reject_reason: Duplicate: a close-up detail of the same mosaic as wga:zearly/1/4mosaics/2ravenna/4nuovo/2south5 (Christ enthroned between four angels, Sant'Apollinare Nuovo, Ravenna), which shows the whole composition.
notes: Commons file 'Christus Ravenna.jpg'; the title 'Christ surrounded by angels and saints' and the artist 'Master of Sant'Apollinare' are generic.

set.l: Triumphal arch, Santi Cosma e Damiano, Rome

summary: In a blue medallion on a gold ground, a white lamb lies on a jewelled throne before a tall golden cross; on the footstool below rests the scroll sealed with seven seals, and jewelled candlesticks with flames stand to either side. This is the Lamb of the Apocalypse, Christ slain and victorious, who alone is worthy to open the scroll of history. At the summit of the arch it greets the faithful before they see the great apse mosaic of Christ's return.
facts: The Lamb is flanked by seven candlesticks, four angels and the four creatures that are also the symbols of the evangelists.
The 24 elders who once offered their crowns to the Lamb were largely lost in the 17th-century rebuilding of the church; only some arms and wreaths survive.
Pope Felix IV turned the building into a church in 527, but the arch mosaics may be 6th century or later, perhaps 7th.

links.label: Medieval Mosaics: Rome, SS Cosmas and Damian

notes: WGA places this detail in the apse; it is on the triumphal arch. Dating of the arch relative to the apse (c. 530) is uncertain.
